#1  Hurricane Isaias · AL092026 · Adv 13A 110 mph

Type & strengthHurricane Isaias — 110 mph (Cat 2), 967 mb
ISAIAS NEARING LANDFALL IN THE WESTERN FLORIDA PANHANDLE
Weakening is expected after landfall, and Isaias is forecast to become post-tropical on Saturday. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from the center and tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 205 miles (335 km).
Position (now)30.1°N 86.6°W at Fri Oct 9, 8:00 PM ET
about 45 mi SE of Pensacola Florida
about 95 mi ESE of Mobile Alabama

On the forecast track, Isaias is expected to make landfall along the coast of the western Florida Panhandle within the next hour or two.

Key hazards
  • Storm Surge: The combination of a dangerous storm surge and the tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded by rising waters moving inland from the shoreline. The water could reach the following heights above ground somewhere in the indicated areas if the peak surge occurs at the time of high tide... AL/FL Border to Grayton Beach, FL...6-9 ft Grayton Beach, FL to Indian Pass, FL...4-7 ft Indian Pass, FL to Steinhatchee River, FL...4-6 ft Dauphin Island, AL to AL/FL Border...4-6 ft Steinhatchee River, FL to Suwannee River, FL...3-5 ft Mouth of the Mississippi River, LA to Dauphin Island, AL...3-5 ft Lower Mobile Bay...3-5 ft Suwannee River, FL to Yankeetown, FL...2-4 ft Upper Mobile Bay...2-4 ft The deepest water will occur along the immediate coast in areas of onshore winds, where the surge will be accompanied by large and dangerous waves. Surge-related flooding depends on the relative timing of the surge and the tidal cycle, and can vary greatly over short distances. For information specific to your area, please see products issued by your local National Weather Service forecast office. For a complete depiction of areas at risk of storm surge inundation, please see the National Weather Service Peak Storm Surge Graphic, available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?peakSurge.
  • Wind: Hurricane conditions are expected this evening into early Saturday within the Hurricane Warning area. Hurricane-force winds are expected to spread inland as far as 100 miles from the coast into southern Alabama. Tropical storm conditions are also occurring in the tropical storm warning areas.
  • Rainfall: From Friday through the weekend, Isaias is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend, and southwest Georgia. Localized totals up to 15 inches are possible, particularly within banding across the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend. Across much of the remainder of the Southeast, rainfall amounts of 2 to 5 inches are expected. Localized higher amounts up to 10 inches are possible, especially across the Southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas. Flash, urban, and river flooding is possible across the region, with considerable impacts likely across much of southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle into southwestern Georgia. Considerable flash flooding and landslides are also possible across the Southern Appalachians. For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with Isaias, please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall Graphic available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?rainqpf and the Flash Flood Risk graphic at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ero.
  • Tornadoes: The risk for tornadoes will continue into this evening and tonight across the Florida Panhandle, southeast Alabama, and southern Georgia. The tornado threat will continue Saturday across parts of eastern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, Georgia, and the Carolinas.
  • Surf: Swells from Isaias are affecting much of the Gulf coasts of the United States, Mexico, and western Cuba. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions. Please consult products from your local weather office. A depiction of rip current risk for the United States can be found at: hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ripCurrents

Some strengthening is possible the next day or so, but rapid weakening forecast after the storm moves inland over the southwestern United States on Sunday. Tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 80 miles (130 km) from the center.

Key hazards
  • Wind: Tropical storm conditions are expected to reach portions of western Baja California within the Tropical Storm Warning area starting Saturday evening or night. Tropical storm conditions are also possible within the Tropical Storm Watch area in extreme Southern California and eastern Baja California beginning late Saturday night or early Sunday. Strong gusty winds associated with the system are expected to spread over interior portions of the Southwest United States, especially in areas of higher terrain, from this weekend into early next week.
  • Rainfall: Rachel will bring 1 to 3 inches of rain to portions of Baja California this weekend. Rachel and associated moisture of the system will also bring rainfall of 1 to 3 inches, with maximum amounts locally up to 5 inches in portions of the Southwest United States this weekend. This will lead to increasing coverage of rainfall and potential for flash and urban flooding. For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with Rachel, please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall Graphic available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_ep3.shtml?rainqpf and the Flash Flood Risk graphic at hurricanes.gov/graphics_ep3.shtml?ero.
  • Surf: Swells partly generated by Rachel will build along the coast of Southern California and northern Baja California through the weekend. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions, as well as moderate to isolated major coastal flooding, through early next week.

Key hazards
  • Wind: Hurricane conditions are expected in the Hurricane Warning area Saturday evening or Sunday, with tropical storm conditions expected as soon as Saturday morning. Hurricane conditions are possible in the Hurricane Watch area beginning Sunday afternoon, with tropical storm conditions possible as soon as Sunday morning. Tropical storm conditions are possible within the Tropical Storm Watch area beginning tonight or early Saturday.
  • Rainfall: Simon is expected to produce rainfall totals of 10 to 20 inches over portions of southwestern Mexico, with isolated maximum totals of 30 inches possible across portions of Michoacan, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit through Sunday. This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain. For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with Simon, please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall Graphic available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_ep5.shtml?rainqpf.
  • Storm Surge: A dangerous storm surge is likely along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall. Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves.
  • Surf: Swells generated by Simon will affect portions of the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico during the next few days. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions. Please consult products from your local weather office.

Work with us — Advertise & Sponsor

FR-STORM is a free, independent hurricane dashboard for the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts, refreshed every 3 hours from official NHC / NWS / JTWC data. If you'd like to support it or reach its readers, these are the options:

  • Sponsor this dashboard — your name or logo shown here as “Sponsored by…”, plus a line in the page footer.
  • Advertising placement (banner or card) — a clearly labelled banner or card in this section only.
  • Storm-season local business sponsorship (Gulf / Atlantic coast) — for local businesses that want to support hurricane-season readiness along the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
  • Other partnership / service offer — data, tools, services or other ideas.

Ground rules: sponsor and advertising content appears only in this section and the page footer, always labelled “Sponsor”. It is never placed inside the storm cards, maps, alerts or the official NHC / NWS information, and sponsors have no say in the storm information. Pricing and audience details are shared on request — none are published here.

Sources & how this was made

Why this page exists

It is a free, independent hurricane check focused on the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts. It puts the threat first: is anything likely to affect land within 72 hours, where and when — then the rest of the Atlantic, Pacific and West Pacific for context.

How it is built

  1. Every 3 hours a scheduled job runs refresh_storm_dash.sh on a private workstation.
  2. Python scripts download the official products listed below straight from NOAA's National Hurricane Center (NHC/CPHC), the National Weather Service (NWS) and the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) — text advisories, outlooks and the NHC GIS shapefiles (cone, track, forecast points, past track, outlook areas, watch/warning lines).
  3. The scripts rank systems by threat to the US / Florida, draw the static maps, and build this page. The interactive map's shapes are embedded in the page at build time (no live data calls), so it is a snapshot as of the pulled time shown.
  4. The page is published to GitHub Pages (a static web host) and checked live after each refresh.

Translation, units and time zones

Any language: the language picker at the top uses the Google Website Translator — this is machine translation by Google, done in your browser, and it can be wrong. The English text is the official version (copied from NHC / NWS / JTWC); if anything is unclear, use the English page or the official NHC products. Storm names, advisory numbers, storm IDs, coordinates and source URLs are marked do not translate. If the translator widget can't load, the Open translated page link opens a Google Translate copy of this page instead. Your language choice is remembered in this browser (localStorage) and re-applied on every refresh.

Units and times: NHC publishes winds in mph and knots, pressure in millibars (mb = hPa) and times in Eastern Time. The unit buttons (wind mph / km/h / kt, distance mi / km, pressure mb / hPa / inHg) and the extra local-time display are converted in your browser from those official values; the default is US units for US-English browsers and metric elsewhere.

Official vs. calculated

  • Official (copied from NHC/NWS/JTWC): storm positions, winds, pressure, movement, forecast points and times, cones, outlook areas and formation odds, watches/warnings, wind-speed probabilities, NWS alerts and discussion text.
  • Calculated by this dashboard (not official): plain-language positions ("about 400 mi W of…"), estimated coast-crossing times interpolated between NHC forecast points, threat ranking and the CLEAR / MONITOR / WATCH / WARNING status labels (those labels follow NWS watches/warnings when any exist).
  • Duplicate check: when an outlook invest (e.g. Invest AL92) becomes an advisory storm (e.g. TD Nine, AL09), the old invest entry is dropped automatically. Nothing needed dropping this run.
  • Fetch problems this run: none — every source above downloaded and parsed.

Limitations

  • This is not an official warning source. It can be up to 3 hours old, a download can fail, and parsing can be wrong. Always follow the National Hurricane Center (nhc.noaa.gov), your local National Weather Service office (weather.gov) and your county emergency management (evacuation zones, shelters: ready.gov/hurricanes).
  • The cone shows where the storm's center will probably go — not how big the storm is. Surge, wind and rain often reach far outside it.
  • Formation odds are chances a depression or storm forms, not landfall odds. Disturbances have no official track until NHC starts advisories.
  • Times are converted to Eastern Time (your local time can be shown next to them). GTWO outlook GIS stamp: Fri Oct 9, 7:17 PM ET.
  • Translations are machine-made by Google and may be wrong; the English NHC/NWS wording is the official text.

Odds are NHC tropical-cyclone formation chances, not landfall chances. NHC winds are 1-min sustained as published (mph); JTWC knots are converted to mph.
